    Styling the Dashboard

    Last updated on 2026-11-19 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do you set a dashboard’s overall look with a built-in theme and add a logo?
    • How do you choose value box colours that match your theme?
    • How do you style charts and format numbers consistently?

    Objectives

    • Set a dashboard’s overall look using a built-in theme and add a logo in the YAML header
    • Choose value box colours that match the chosen theme
    • Apply a consistent ggplot2 theme and your own OA colours to charts
    • Format large numbers consistently using format()

    Time to make it look good

    In the skeleton episode, we deliberately left styling for later. Now is the time.

    Choosing a theme and adding a logo

    Quarto dashboards come with built-in themes (based on a project called Bootswatch). Each one changes fonts, colours and spacing across the whole dashboard with a single YAML setting. A logo is shown next to the title in the navigation bar. Both are settings of the dashboard format, so they go inside dashboard:, indented one level further, just like orientation before:

    YAML 

    ---
title: "Open Access Monitoring Dashboard"
format:
  dashboard:
    theme: morph
    logo: images/lc_logo.svg
---

    First, create an images folder in your project (the same way you created data earlier), download the Library Carpentry Logo and move the file into it. The path in logo: is relative to your project folder. Render the dashboard to see the new look.

    You can browse the full list of themes, with previews, in the Quarto theming documentation. Try a few and see which fits your institution.

    Matching value box colours to the theme

    Recall the color option of the value boxes (primary, success, warning, info). These names refer to a fixed set of colour roles defined by Bootstrap, the framework dashboards are built on: primary, secondary, success, info, warning, danger, light and dark. Whichever theme you choose defines what each role looks like, so your value boxes automatically match the theme, without looking up colour codes. If you need a colour outside this set, you can use, for example, hex code colors.

    Callout

    Colours carry meaning

    Be consistent: if green means “open” on one card, it should not mean “closed” on another. Pick colours once and reuse them.

    Styling charts to match

    Your ggplot2 charts do not automatically pick up the dashboard’s theme. They need their own styling. Two small additions make a big difference.

    A built-in ggplot2 theme, added with + like other layers. theme_minimal() removes the grey background and gridlines, which fits dashboard cards well:

    R 

    oa_df |>
  group_by(publication_year) |>
  summarise(oa_share = mean(is_oa) * 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(publication_year), y = oa_share)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Publication year", y = "Open access share (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

    Your own OA colours. Remember the named vector oa_colors from the R episode? Named vectors are exactly what the scale_fill_manual() function from ggplot2 needs: each OA status gets its colour. Define the vector in your setup chunk, with one entry for each OA status that occurs in your data (check count(oa_status) from the data episode):

    R 

    oa_colors <- c(
  gold = "gold",
  hybrid = "orange",
  green = "forestgreen",
  bronze = "chocolate",
  diamond = "skyblue",
  closed = "grey"
)

    The named vector oa_colors is used inside a chart that colours the bars by status. For this chart, we need the share of each OA status per publication year. We count the articles per year and status, calculate each status’s share within its year, and map oa_status to the bar colour with fill = oa_status:

    R 

    oa_df |>
  count(publication_year, oa_status) |>
  group_by(publication_year) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n) * 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(publication_year), y = share, fill = oa_status)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = oa_colors) +
  labs(x = "Publication year", y = "Share of articles (%)", fill = "OA status") +
  theme_minimal()

    Formatting numbers consistently

    For value boxes (and anywhere else you display a large number), a comma as thousands separator makes numbers easier to read at a glance: 1810861 versus 1,810,861. The format() function with its big.mark argument does this:

    R 

    format(nrow(oa_df), big.mark = ",")

    Wrap it around the value in the “Total Publications” box:

    R 

    #| content: valuebox
#| title: "Total Publications"
#| icon: book
#| color: primary

format(nrow(oa_df), big.mark = ",")
    Challenge

    Challenge: Apply the styling everywhere

    Go through your dashboard and check:

    1. The count value boxes (“Total Publications”, “Open Access Publications”) are wrapped in format(..., big.mark = ",").
    2. The charts have theme_minimal() added.
    3. You chose a theme and added the logo to the YAML header.

    Render once more and check that everything looks consistent.

    Key Points

    • Set theme and logo inside dashboard: in the YAML header to style the whole dashboard at once
    • Value box color options (primary, success, warning, …) automatically match your theme
    • ggplot2 charts need their own styling, such as theme_minimal()
    • A named vector of colours, passed to scale_fill_manual(), gives each OA status a consistent colour
    • format(x, big.mark = ",") adds thousands separators to numbers you display
